feedback.problem:
Consider the initial value problem 

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}x+2,\,y(0)=-1.
$$

Use the tangent line approximation of $y(x)$ at $x=0$ to approximate $y(0.5).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $y(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =y(a)+{y}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =y(0)+{y}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

From the initial condition, we know that $y(0)=-1.$ We also know that ${y}^{′}(x)={y}^{2}x+2,$ so

$$
{y}^{′}(0)=(-1)^{2}\cdot 0+2=2.
$$

Substituting our values for $y(0)$ and ${y}^{′}(0)$ into our expression for $L(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =y(0)+{y}^{′}(0)(x-0) \\  & =-1+(2)(x-0) \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can approximate $y(0.5)$ using $L(0.5).$ We get

$$
y(0.5)≈L(0.5)=2(0.5)-1=0.
$$
